blockers.summary: Regression mentioned: "…o ensure this does not happen? - If a regression were to occur, what would it look like to users? How would they know?…" (mruffell)

The submitter reports that the proposed package (22.03.8-0ubuntu0.22.04.2) refreshes flows on upgrade. That is the LP #1940043 regression the --restart flag was meant to prevent. A new fix is promised but not yet delivered, and there is no verification-done for jammy or yoga.

The reviewer asked for the SRU template to be revised: a clearer user-visible impact, a test case for the preinstall script that checks runtime state is preserved on upgrade, and a 'where problems could occur' section explaining how LP #1940043 is avoided and what a regression would look like. There are two standing issues with these patches:

- get_global_pool_hard_max_size parses /proc/sys/vm/max_map_count incorrectly, resulting in the default value being used unconditionally

blockers.summary: Regression mentioned: "…to 64. This could produce a performance regression for some users, as the performance bottleneck of this cap was significant enoug…" (whershberger)

The backported patches parse /proc/sys/vm/max_map_count incorrectly, so the default value is always used and the system limit is never taken into account. The upstream fix is submitted but not merged, and the SRU does not yet carry it.

The default returned by get_global_pool_hard_max_size is UINT_MAX, so the hard cap is effectively disabled. A conservative default such as 65530 is needed. This fix is also unmerged upstream, so the SRU needs to carry it.

Reading /proc/sys/vm/max_map_count needs a libvirt AppArmor change (LP #2170732). Without it, and without a versioned Breaks in qemu to force the libvirt upgrade, QEMU under libvirt may be denied access to the file and fall back to the default. The libvirt fix and the Breaks relationship are not yet confirmed in place.

The fix only reduces the chance of exhausting max_map_count and does not eliminate it. With very large vCPU counts, a crash remains reproducible: a 255-vCPU guest still crashed under the noble limit of 1048576 with 'failed to set up stack guard page'. The remaining behaviour at the limit is not clearly documented or tested.

The reviewer's question remains unresolved: noble's kernel already has a much higher default limit and does not hit this crash in typical cases, so the regression risk and the justification for the SRU are unclear. The impact analysis has also shifted several times (vCPU thread-local caches, IOThreads, and migration threads, which are unexplored).
